items.title: Frank Foster interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 7, 1998
items.q: Comparing it to Coltrane or something?

ctx.x: He certainly doesn’t and he still lives in a hotel. But this Jazz Spotlight News was, I think, a very worthwhile venture in which everybody who contributed talked about the music and the field and the business, the affairs of music, just the way they felt. You know they weren’t politically motivated to lean toward one side or the other, they’d — straight ahead, exactly how they felt, pulling no punches. And when I wrote this article, “I’ll never make it big because my stuff is just too old fashioned,” was based…
Comparing it to Coltrane or something? Or the avant garde or free jazz?
The avant garde, free jazz, funk, rock & roll.

items.title: Frank Foster — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I took some photos of him when we were on tour together.

ctx.x: Just talk about Coltrane for a minute.

I didn’t know him on an intimate basis, because we never got together to talk at length, but we knew each other to greet each other in public. I took some photos of him when we were on tour together. We were on tour together. We were on a single concert in Hamburg, Germany, at one time. The most significant thing about John Coltrane, my memories of John Coltrane, was the time John Coltrane was playing at the Village Gate or the Five Spot. The Count Basie orchestra was playing at the Jazz Gallery during that same…

the direction of this club where Trane was playing. We were rushing. We wanted to get there so we could have time to hear him for a few minutes and get back before our intermission was over. Halfway between the Jazz Gallery and I’ll say the Five Spot where Trane was playing, we ran into Trane and a couple of his fellows. They said, “Where are you guys going?” We said, “We’re coming to hear you.” He said, “Oh, shit, we’re coming to hear you.” So it says that Trane himself was listening -- while I’m listening to…

items.title: Frank Foster and Bill Hughes interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Schenectady, New York, March 28, 1995
items.q: they even use Coltrane’s son, Ravi Coltrane with Elvin Jones

ctx.x: Could you name a couple of those groups?

Young groups, you know like Terrance Blanchard, of course the Elvin Jones group makes use of a lot of youngsters such as Nicholas Payton and they even use Coltrane’s son, Ravi Coltrane with Elvin Jones. And of course Vincent Herring, an alto saxophonist, Jesse Davis, another alto saxophonist, Bobby Watson, another alto saxophonist, Roy Hargrove, Chris McBride, Antonio Hart. These are the youngsters that are, that are carrying on authentic jazz. This is not the Basie style, now, I’m talking about small group jazz.…
No, not necessarily doing the Basie thing, but in other words, just putting your thumb on the pulse and saying, are the traditions alive and well?
